answer: The question's premise is partly incorrect. Node2vec does not rely only on immediate neighborhoods. It learns embeddings from second-order biased random walks, with parameters p and q interpolating between breadth-first (local, closer to structural equivalence) and depth-first (broader, closer to homophily) exploration. It is also not trained on a dataset chosen specifically to evaluate structural equivalence in citation graphs. It is unsupervised and runs on whatever graph is provided. In the original paper (Grover & Leskovec, 2016), the structural-equivalence illustration used the Les Misérables character co-appearance network. Its experiments used BlogCatalog, PPI (protein-protein interaction), and Wikipedia co-occurrence networks for multi-label node classification, and Facebook, PPI, arXiv collaboration (ASTRO-PH, HEP-TH) networks for link prediction. The arXiv and HEP-TH collaboration networks are the closest citation-like datasets used.
confidence_reasoning: I am fairly confident about node2vec's biased random walk design and the core datasets, but less certain of the exact dataset list and which graph was used for the structural-equivalence illustration.
